You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: New Highs! Semiconductor Equipment Stocks Surge Collectively: AI Boom + Korea’s $800B Mega Order Ignites AMAT, LRCX, KLAC

TEXT:
Current Market Momentum: Korea’s Massive Investment Sparks Equipment Stocks, Big Three Hit Fresh Highs
1. The U.S. semiconductor equipment sector has been red-hot recently. At the end of June, AMAT (Applied Materials) surged nearly 10% in a single day, hitting a record high with a monthly gain exceeding 50%. LRCX (Lam Research) rose nearly 6%, and KLAC (KLA) climbed over 7% — all three refreshing their recent peaks.
The immediate catalyst is Korea’s blockbuster move: Samsung and SK Hynix plan to invest about 800 trillion KRW in the southwest to build four advanced chip fabs, aiming to double DRAM capacity within five years.
This massive capital expenditure starts with equipment purchases — from front-end wafer fabrication to back-end optimization for AI chips. Global top-tier equipment makers stand to benefit directly. Market sentiment ignited instantly, with capital chasing these “shovel sellers,” driving up volume and volatility.
2. Investment Thesis: AI Data Center Demand Explodes, WFE Spending Forecasts Sharply Upgraded
This rally isn’t just hype — it’s driven by a real industry cycle.
AI, especially agentic AI, has triggered explosive demand for high-performance chips and storage in data centers. Global hyperscalers are expected to pour over $600 billion into AI infrastructure in 2026, with semiconductors accounting for 95%+ of an AI server rack’s value.
On the memory side, structural NAND demand has surged, forcing fabs to expand and upgrade capacity. Citi recently raised its global wafer fab equipment (WFE) spending forecasts significantly: $145 billion in 2026, $200 billion in 2027, and $250 billion in 2028 under the bull case — the firm’s first-ever 2028 outlook, signaling strong long-term confidence.
The three major equipment players each have distinct strengths but are all perfectly positioned along this wave:
AMAT has the broadest equipment portfolio, leads in advanced packaging, and builds customer stickiness through software subscriptions — ideal for capturing full-chain benefits.
LRCX excels in etch and deposition, especially benefiting from complex storage process iterations.
KLAC dominates process control and metrology (nearly monopolistic position), as yield enhancement is essential for every new production line.
With customer capex recovering and order visibility improving, earnings growth visibility is much stronger than in previous cycle troughs. For traders, these names typically offer high volatility and strong elasticity when market risk appetite rises.
3. In-Depth Breakdown of the Top 3 Beneficiaries: AMAT, LRCX, KLAC Each Have Their Edge
AMAT — The All-Rounder “Shovel Master” Beyond traditional deposition, etch, and CMP processes, AMAT holds advantages in advanced packaging and display equipment. Facing surging demand for advanced nodes in AI chips, its diversified layout allows it to capture opportunities across both logic and memory expansion. Its recent stock performance has been the strongest, reflecting market recognition of its growth elasticity.
LRCX — Storage Cycle Specialist LRCX focuses on etch equipment. As NAND and DRAM structures grow more complex, both replacement and new demand are robust. Citi and other institutions are bullish on its NAND equipment share gains. With expansions in Korea and Taiwan landing, 2026–2027 earnings acceleration looks promising. Higher volatility but greater upside — perfect for storage-themed investors.
KLAC — Deep Moat Leader With ~60% market share in process control and metrology equipment, KLAC enjoys high technical barriers and a wide gap over the #2 player. Every new fab line needs its tools for yield control. Recent dividend hikes, upcoming stock split, and share buybacks signal strong management confidence.
The three companies are not competitors but complementary players that together form the core of the semiconductor manufacturing equipment supply chain. Following the major direction of AI capex, they offer near-term event catalysts and solid mid-term earnings support.
4. Summary
The current heat in semiconductor equipment is fundamentally driven by AI infrastructure moving from concept to large-scale deployment. Korea’s mega order is just the latest spark — the real story is the long-term global data center expansion trend.
AMAT, LRCX, and KLAC , as sector leaders, boast strong fundamentals and high order visibility, making them prime picks to ride this prosperity cycle.
That said, markets carry risks — geopolitical tensions, shifts in customer capex pace, and other factors deserve close attention. Combine the latest fundamentals, industry data, and your own position sizing for rational participation.
Whether in spot or leveraged products, keep a close eye on these three names to capture alpha in the equipment space. Don’t miss the “sell shovels” opportunity in the AI supply chain!
